books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: Goods moved both ways, but Native peoples bore the epidemics and forced labor while Europeans gained most.
Judged by modern standards of consent and free trade, the transfer was voluntary exchange on both sides.
options.misconception: It judges a 16th-century system built on conquest by modern free-market ideas, as if coercion and choice were the same.

options.text: Potatoes transformed European diets and fed population growth, proving the exchange raised living standards everywhere.
options.misconception: It takes one crop's effect on Europe and stretches it to both sides of the Atlantic.

options.text: Disease alone caused the collapse of Native populations, so the only harm was a biological accident no one intended.
options.misconception: It makes disease the one and only cause, leaving out Spanish violence, enslavement, and uprooted communities.

rationales.general:
1. Open two ledgers. Crops, animals, and diseases really did move in both directions.
2. Ask who paid. Epidemics and forced labor fell overwhelmingly on Native peoples.
3. Ask who gained. Europeans captured most of the food and wealth the exchange produced.
4. Rule out the rest. Disease was not the only harm, the transfer was not voluntary, and one crop does not prove shared prosperity.
Remember: to evaluate a claim about shared benefits, ask who paid and who gained.
rationales.A: The exchange really moved goods both ways, but the costs and the gains were not shared. That is the qualification the argument needs.
rationales.B: A system built on conquest cannot be judged by modern free-market ideas. Coercion is not the same as choice.
rationales.C: One crop's effect on Europe does not prove shared prosperity. It says nothing about what Native peoples paid.
rationales.D: Disease was not the only harm. Spanish violence, enslavement, and uprooted communities also destroyed Native peoples.

stem: A historian argues that the Columbian Exchange was an exchange of goods between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that spread prosperity to people on both sides of the Atlantic. Which response to this argument is most defensible?
